newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - France's National Front in tense election campaign.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - France's National Front in tense election campaign.

text.p: Sticking posters can be dangerous in the southern French town of Vitrolles where the far-right National Front (FN) is fighting to win its fourth city hall in an election next month.
The driver of Socialist candidate Jean-Jacques Anglade had a pot of glue land on his head and suffered face burns while campaigning in this fast-growing industrial town near Marseille.
The incident was the latest of a series of confrontations between supporters of each side, who have been trading insults and occasionally blows.

The National Front, whose candidate is the wife of Bruno Megret, the deputy of fiery FN leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, has recently been forced by a court ruling to take down posters which proclaimed Anglade had been charged with fraud .
Anglade filed a complaint, arguing that he had merely been placed under investigation and not charged.
Two people -- one in each camp -- have been slightly injured and many fear things might get worse as the election nears.
Megret was beaten by Anglade in his bid to become mayor of the town in June 1995. Megret was later declared ineligible for exceeding the legal limit of spending during his campaign.
A court then cancelled the election altogether on evidence that Anglade had abusively urged voters who abstained in the first round of the poll to cast a vote for him in the run-off.

"Those who tried to stop the people of Vitrolles from voting for Megret will now have two (Megrets) instead of one," said Megret, who has convinced his wife Catherine to head the FN's fresh bid against Anglade.
The National Front, which advocates the repatriation of millions of even legal immigrants, captured the southern towns of Toulon, Orange and Marignane in 1995 municipal elections.
Marignane is just around the corner from Vitrolles, where Le Pen's party came close in 1995. Megret lost to Anglade by a mere 353 votes after winning the first round.

Megret, who has named himself spokesman for his wife's campaign, has delivered several speeches in which he promised the National Front would, if elected, fight immigration, tackle crime and bring down the area's high unemployment.
Le Pen, who advocates giving French citizens preference over foreigners for jobs and other state benefits, recently caused an outcry by espousing racial inequality.
Shunned by mainstream politicians, the xenophobic National Front sees the Vitrolles vote as a key test of strength ahead of 1998 general elections.
Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in France's 1995 presidential election but the party has shown even greater strength in some parts of the country, notably the south and the northeast.
In posters plastered across Vitrolles, Megret appears with his wife standing in the background, and the slogan reads "Vote Megret" with no mention of a first name.
"I'm not a politician but an angry spouse," said Catherine Megret. "I'm not running to replace my husband but to represent him."
Anglade's campaign director Alain Arezki said the Socialist candidate would need help from heavyweight politicians from across the political spectrum to counter the National Front.

"After the first round, the debate will leave Vitrolles and it will be up to (Socialist leader Lionel) Jospin, (Communist leader Robert) Hue and (centre-right Prime minister Alain) Juppe to counter Megret," Arezki said.

"Jean-Jacques Anglade represents Resistance but if the Americans don't come, it will be useless," he added, referring to the participation of United States troops in the Allied forces which freed France in 1944.
